title: Tenant-targeted 'GPU leak' detection + graceful queue-drain automation
creator: Maya Patel
description: Summary: During a hosted API capacity event on 2026-02-27 we observed a tenant-scoped surge that led to GPU pool exhaustion. Existing pool-level throttles and autoscaler hysteresis failed to prevent a sustained queue buildup. Root cause was a regression in admission scoring that allowed long-running prefetch and low-priority batched jobs to queue aggressively for several tenants. This ticket defines detection, mitigation automation, and a safer rollout plan to prevent similar tenant-localized 'GPU leak' events.
postmortem_summary: Timeline: 02/27 03:12 UTC — initial latency spikes; 03:05 — queue depth alarm for pool-a; 03:18 — throttling triggered but misattributed due to per-tenant admission score regression; 03:40 — manual soft-drain applied; 04:05 — capacity stabilized after tenant eviction and autoscaler warm-up. Key contributing factors: (1) mutation in admission scoring logic that underweighted prefetch cost under new batching heuristic; (2) pool-level autoscaler hysteresis too long for fast tenant surges; (3) lack of tenant-level queue health alerts and graceful-drain automation. Immediate mitigations (hotfix): revert admission scoring change (PR #5241), temporary lower autoscaler cooldown to 30s, and a manual tenant backfill block for affected tenants.
steps_taken: Rolled back admission scoring change (github.com/redwood/serving/pull/5241) at 2026-02-27T04:20Z
Applied manual soft-drain to free GPU slots for affected pool (runbook executed: runbook link in related_links)
Lowered autoscaler cooldown from 5m -> 30s for emergency pools (temporary)
Added short-term per-tenant admission cap to stop new prefetch batches for top-5 noisy tenants
root_cause_analysis: Regression in admission scoring: new batching heuristic incorrectly treated prefetch as high-throughput but low-cost work, reducing its admission penalty
Autoscaler hysteresis tuned for noise avoidance caused slow reaction to sudden per-tenant surges
No tenant-scoped queue-length SLO or alerting; existing telemetry aggregated at pool level only
No automated graceful drain to evict speculative, low-priority batches while preserving high-priority requests
action_items: AI-1: Implement tenant-level queue health metrics and alerts (owner: S. Lopez, estimate: 3) — emit per-tenant queue depth, 95p latency, inflight token rate into telemetry. Link: dashboard draft https://dash.redwood.ai/d/queues/tenant-health

AI-2: Add 'soft-drain' orchestration that can evict or demote speculative/prefetch batches by tenant when queue depth > threshold (owner: Carlos Nguyen, estimate: 8) — library + graceful rollback + audit log
AI-3: Harden admission scoring tests: add regression unit + integration tests that synthesize prefetch-heavy workloads (owner: Priya Sharma, estimate: 5) — include CI job and attack test

AI-4: Autoscaler tuning: introduce two-mode hysteresis (rapid emergency mode w/ short cooldown + standard mode w/ longer cooldown) and policy to flip to emergency mode if tenant-local surge detected (owner: Infra Team, estimate: 5)
AI-5: Canary rollout for scoring fix: stage to 10% of pools with synthetic load and tenant-sim tests for 48h before global rollout (owner: Maya Patel, estimate: 2)

AI-6: Incident runbook update: add decision tree for tenant-local surges, including playbook to trigger soft-drain, temporary admission caps, and autoscaler emergency flip (owner: Oncall team, estimate: 1)
AI-7: Post-deploy audit: run chaos/soak test that simulates tenant surge patterns monthly and surface regressions (owner: Reliability Eng, estimate: 3)
acceptance_criteria: Per-tenant queue health metrics are live and alerting when 95p latency > 2s or queue depth > X (X to be determined in design doc)
Soft-drain automation implemented with audit logs and a rollback path; exercised in a staged canary
Admission scoring regression tests added and passing in CI for both unit and integration stages
Autoscaler emergency mode implemented and validated in staging under synthetic tenant surges
Updated runbook published and oncall trained (walkthrough completed)
risks_and_tradeoffs: Aggressive per-tenant caps can degrade throughput for legitimate high-volume tenants — mitigation: prioritize by SLA tier and provide temporary crediting mechanisms
Shortening autoscaler cooldown increases stability risk (oscillation); hence we implement a two-mode approach with damping and safety checks
Soft-drain evicts low-priority work which may increase customer-visible latency for background tasks — will document and add customer notices for enterprise tenants
followups: Followup-1: Measure long-term impact on unit cost after soft-drain and autoscaler changes (report due 2026-04-15)
Followup-2: Product decision on exposing per-tenant throttles to customers vs keeping as internal control (PM: Claire Hsu)
Followup-3: Add tenant surge simulator to the internal loadgen suite and unblock additional CI gates
notes: Design proposal for soft-drain: prefer eviction of speculative/prefetch batches, then demotion to background queue, then hard eviction as last resort
We will not surface per-tenant throttles to self-serve customers until after two production incidents are tested end-to-end
Consider exposing warning webhooks to enterprise tenants when we apply soft-drain to their workloads
